section_titles: Bird Watching — Directions on a Camp Map
periods.activity_title: Your Body Is a Compass: Directions in Space

tasks_in_class.description: Manu faces the rising Sun; fill: that direction is ___, left hand points ___ direction, right hand points ___ direction; which way is west?
Read clues about tent positions (west of road, closest to lake, north of green, south of lake); colour tents accordingly; draw a tent east of the lake.
Write the directions of window, bed, cupboard, and bedside table in relation to the girl in the room diagram.
Make a drawing of your room; locate directions of things from the centre; draw the direction arrow for your room.

homework.description: Write the names of things placed in East, West, North, and South directions in your room.

time_bands.activity: Children stand, face the window where the morning Sun comes from, and name East aloud; they stretch arms to name North and South, then solve p.171 ("Manu faces the rising Sun; fill that direction is….")

Pairs read the camp map and work through Bird Watching!, p.172 ("Read clues about tent positions…"), colouring tents and drawing the east-of-lake tent; the class pools answers and reconciles any differences.
Children read the room diagram and complete Map of a Room, p.172 ("Write the directions of window, bed, cupboard…."); teacher asks how they decided a direction without standing in the room.
Children sketch their own room freehand and complete Map of a Room, p.173 ("Make a drawing of your room; locate directions…."); two volunteers share their drawings and explain one directional choice.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse left and right with North and South once they rotate away from facing East — anchor every check to 'face the Sun first.' The shift from body-anchored direction to reading a top-down map is the conceptual step in the bird-watching task; let pairs argue it out before confirming. Map of a Room, p.173 Q5 (writing things in each direction from their own room) works well as an at-home task since children need to stand in their actual room.

section_titles: Zoo Trip — Street Map and Bus Route
periods.activity_title: Reading a Street Map: Roads, Routes, and Neighbours

tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks: bus goes north from parking, turns right onto ___ Road driving ___ direction to reach S1; turns right/left onto ___ Road driving ___ direction to reach S2.
(a) Houses east of Jaideep's; (b) route from Ravi's house to children's park; (c) stop closer to Lali's house; (d) route for Golu to nearest stop; (e) direction for Prem to reach Stop 2.

time_bands.activity: Whole class studies the street map on p.174 together; children name the three roads, find the compass rose, and trace the bus route with a finger before any writing begins.

Children individually complete Bus Route, p.174 ("Fill blanks: bus goes north from parking, turns right onto ___ Road…."); teacher circulates and asks 'which direction is the bus facing after it turns?'
Small groups work through Bus Route, p.174 parts (a)–(e) ("Houses east of Jaideep's; route from Ravi's house…."); each group assigns one sub-question to report back on.
Groups share answers to (b) and (e); class discusses whether two different routes for (b) are both valid, cementing the idea that direction is relative to the map's compass rose.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is treating 'turn right' as always meaning 'face East' — help children see that 'right' depends on the direction the bus is currently facing. Sub-questions (b) and (d) have more than one valid route; accept any correct sequence of road names and directions. The map has named roads and a compass rose; make sure children find both before solving.

periods.activity_title: Metro Map: Reading a Legend and Planning Routes

tasks_in_class.description: Read the key; identify symbols on the metro map; name what different coloured lines represent; mark Qutb Minar on Yellow Line and Supreme Court on Blue Line.
(a) Trace different routes Qutb Minar→Supreme Court; (b) Lali's suggestion — which stations to change line again; (c) route with least stations; (d) best route to zoo from Qutb Minar.

homework.description: Make a map of school with key for symbols; hide objects; mark positions with red dots/flags; challenge friends to find hidden things using the map.

time_bands.activity: Children open to p.175 and read the key together; teacher asks 'what does a circle mean? what does a colour mean?' before children mark Qutb Minar and Supreme Court per Delhi Metro Train Stations, p.175 ("Read the key; identify symbols….")

Pairs trace two or more routes from Qutb Minar to Supreme Court and record them, then work through Delhi Metro Train Stations, p.176 parts (a)–(d) ("Trace different routes Qutb Minar→Supreme Court…."); partners compare their chosen 'best route' and the reason.

Three pairs share contrasting routes; class counts stations and interchanges together to evaluate which is shorter in stations and which has fewer line changes, discussing what 'best' means in each case.
Teacher introduces Let Us Do, p.176 ("Make a map of school with key for symbols….") as an at-home challenge; children note what symbols they will use for doors, windows, and trees.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently count every station they pass through rather than just interchange stations for part (b); model the distinction by tracing one route slowly. 'Best route' in part (d) is intentionally open — children should state their criterion (fewest stations, fewest changes) and the answer will differ; both are valid. The school-map task works best when children sketch it from memory at home and bring it to share.

section_titles: Anthill in the Zoo — Grid Distances and Directions
periods.activity_title: Ant Trails: Describing Paths with Distance and Direction

tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks: distance and direction for ant to reach sugar (b), bread (c — two segments), apple (d — three segments); identify other routes to apple and which is shortest.

time_bands.activity: Children examine the anthill grid on p.177; teacher asks them to point to the anthill, count the grid squares to sugar along one direction, and agree on units before any writing.

Children work individually on Anthill in the Zoo, p.177 ("Fill blanks: distance and direction for ant to reach sugar (b), bread (c)…."), starting with the single-segment path to sugar, then the two-segment path to bread.
Children tackle the three-segment path to apple (d) and then find at least one alternative route to apple; pairs compare routes and count total segments to argue which is shortest.

Class shares two or three different routes to apple; teacher records direction-distance sentences on the board, drawing attention to how the same destination can be reached by different ordered paths.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often write direction before checking whether the grid line actually runs that way — insist they trace with a finger before writing. The key insight for the open-ended part is that 'shortest' means fewest total centimetres, not fewest turns; let children debate this. Connecting cm on the grid to real distance measurement reinforces the idea that map grids use a standard unit.

periods.activity_title: Zoo Coordinates: Ordered Pairs on a Grid Map

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo), p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Fill blanks to reach tortoise: steps east→column, steps north→row; state location of tortoise (4,1); identify what is at (1,4).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q1, p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Locate the animal at positions (11,11), (2,6), (6,4), (3,10), (11,3), (10,9) on the zoo grid map.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q2, p.178
tasks_in_class.description: Write the ordered-pair position of Lion, Elephant, Tortoise, Deer, Panda, and Crocodile on the zoo map.

homework.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q3, p.178
homework.description: Place coloured dots at positions (8,3) Red, (2,9) Green, (7,3) Blue, (3,8) Orange, (8,6) Black, (6,6) Pink on the zoo grid.

time_bands.activity: Children read the introductory steps on p.178 and complete Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo), p.178 ("Fill blanks to reach tortoise: steps east→column, steps north→row…."); class confirms the rule — east first, then north — before moving on.

Children individually work through Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q1, p.178 ("Locate the animal at positions (11,11), (2,6)…."); teacher circulates and asks 'which number do you move first?'

Children complete Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q2, p.178 ("Write the ordered-pair position of Lion, Elephant…."); pairs check each other's coordinates by reversing — using the partner's pair to find the animal.

Teacher introduces Q3 as an at-home task, p.178 ("Place coloured dots at positions (8,3) Red, (2,9) Green…."); two children explain in their own words what the first and second numbers in a pair each mean.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error is reading the row number before the column — (4,1) is read as '4 north, then 1 east' instead of '4 east, then 1 north'; the body-direction work from the cardinal direction activities supports the correct sequence. Q1 and Q2 together form a reversible pair: finding an animal from its pair and writing the pair of a named animal; this mutual-checking activity surfaces errors naturally. Q3 (placing coloured dots) is well suited as an at-home task since it requires crayons and unhurried grid work.
materials: Coloured crayons or pencils (for Q3 at home)

items.prompt: Draw a simple room shape. Place a door on the South wall, a window on the East wall, and a bed in the North-West corner. Then draw an arrow to show North on your map.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A room shape with a door marked on the South wall, a window on the East wall, a bed in the North-West corner, and a North arrow pointing upward (or in a consistent direction the student labels N).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fix one direction first (North arrow), then place each object relative to that direction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use their body (face East, stretch arms) before drawing; stretch: add one more object and name its direction from the centre.

exercise.description: Make a drawing of your room; locate directions of things from the centre; draw the direction arrow for your room.

items.prompt: On a metro map, a coloured line with circles at intervals is used. What does each circle most likely represent?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the map's key to match each symbol to its meaning.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The child confuses underground features with station symbols, not using the legend.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child is mixing bus-route map conventions with metro map conventions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child is guessing a road-map meaning for a metro map symbol without reading the key.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: point the child to the key and ask them to find the circle symbol there; stretch: ask them to name two other symbols in the key and say what they represent.

exercise.description: Read the key; identify symbols on the metro map; name what different coloured lines represent; mark Qutb Minar on Yellow Line and Supreme Court on Blue Line.

items.prompt: Priya faces the rising Sun in the morning. Which direction is behind her?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: West. When Priya faces East (the rising Sun), the direction behind her is West.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the body-compass rule: face East (rising Sun), and the direction opposite — behind you — is West.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child confuses the direction to the left (North) with the direction behind.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child may know North and South are perpendicular but has not applied the facing rule correctly.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child is naming the direction Priya faces rather than the direction behind her.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to stand and physically face the window where the Sun rises, then point behind them; stretch: ask what direction is to their left and to their right from the same position.

exercise.description: Manu faces the rising Sun; fill: that direction is ___, left hand points ___ direction, right hand points ___ direction; which way is west?

items.section_title: Bird Watching — Directions on a Camp Map
items.prompt: On a camp map, the lake is in the centre. Tent A is west of the lake and Tent B is north of the lake. If you walk from Tent A to Tent B, in which direction do you mostly travel? Explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Mostly northward (and a little east). Tent A is directly west and Tent B is directly north of the lake, so moving from A to B means moving to the right (east) and upward (north) on the map — the dominant new direction gained is North.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Locate both tents on the map relative to the centre, then describe the direction from one to the other using the compass rose.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw a quick sketch with the lake in the middle and mark A and B before answering; stretch: ask them to describe the return journey from B to A.

exercise.description: Read clues about tent positions (west of road, closest to lake, north of green, south of lake); colour tents accordingly; draw a tent east of the lake.

items.prompt: Raju stands in the centre of his room. The door is to his East and the wardrobe is to his West. If Raju turns to face the wardrobe, which direction is the door now?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Behind him (East). The door is fixed to the East wall; turning to face West (the wardrobe) puts the East wall — and the door — directly behind Raju.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Objects on a map do not move when a person turns; the door stays East on the room map regardless of which way Raju faces.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child thinks turning changes the cardinal direction of the object, rotating North to where the door now appears.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Same misconception — the child rotates the object's direction with the person's body.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child correctly identifies the door as East on the map but does not account for Raju now facing the opposite direction, so 'East' without 'behind' is incomplete.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child stand, face a wall labelled East, then turn to face West and point to where the East wall is; stretch: ask which direction the window (to Raju's North) is after he turns to face West.

exercise.description: Write the directions of window, bed, cupboard, and bedside table in relation to the girl in the room diagram.

items.section_title: Zoo Trip — Street Map and Bus Route
items.prompt: A bus is travelling South along River Road. At the junction it turns left. In which direction is the bus now travelling? How did you work this out?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: East. When the bus faces South and turns left, it turns to face East.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the facing-direction rule: when facing South, left is East and right is West.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to face South themselves and then turn left to feel the new direction; stretch: ask what direction the bus would face if it then turned right at the next junction.

exercise.description: (a) Houses east of Jaideep's; (b) route from Ravi's house to children's park; (c) stop closer to Lali's house; (d) route for Golu to nearest stop; (e) direction for Prem to reach Stop 2.

items.prompt: Meera wants to travel from Station P (on the Red Line) to Station Q (on the Blue Line). She can change lines only at an interchange station. Name the two things she should check to decide which route is best, and explain why each matters.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She should check (1) the number of stations on each possible route — fewer stations means a shorter journey; and (2) the number of line changes (interchanges) — each change adds waiting and walking time.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare all possible routes by counting stations and interchanges, then choose the route that best balances both.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to name just one thing that makes a route shorter; stretch: ask what she should do if one route has fewer stations but more interchanges than another — which would she choose and why?

exercise.description: (a) Trace different routes Qutb Minar→Supreme Court; (b) Lali's suggestion — which stations to change line again; (c) route with least stations; (d) best route to zoo from Qutb Minar.

items.section_title: Anthill in the Zoo — Grid Distances and Directions
items.prompt: An ant starts at a point on a grid. It crawls 3 cm East, then 2 cm North to reach a piece of food. A second ant takes a different route: 2 cm North, then 3 cm East. Do both ants travel the same total distance? Do they end at the same place? Explain.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, both ants travel the same total distance (3 + 2 = 5 cm). Yes, they end at the same place, because the East segment is always 3 cm and the North segment is always 2 cm — order does not change the final position on a grid.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the segment lengths for total distance; trace both routes on the grid to confirm the endpoint is the same.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to draw both routes on a small grid; stretch: ask whether a third route — 1 cm East, 2 cm North, 2 cm East — also ends at the same place and has the same total distance.

exercise.description: Fill blanks: distance and direction for ant to reach sugar (b), bread (c — two segments), apple (d — three segments); identify other routes to apple and which is shortest.

items.prompt: On a zoo grid map, you move 5 steps East and then 3 steps North from the entrance. Which ordered pair describes your position?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (5, 3). The first number in the ordered pair is the column (East steps = 5) and the second is the row (North steps = 3).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the rule: move East first (column number), then North (row number) — column comes first in the ordered pair.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child reversed the rule, writing North steps first and East steps second.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child used the East value (5) for both numbers, ignoring the North count.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child used the North value (3) for both numbers, ignoring the East count.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: remind the child to say 'East first' aloud before writing the pair; stretch: give the pair (7, 2) and ask them to describe the journey step by step.

exercise.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo), p.178
exercise.description: Fill blanks to reach tortoise: steps east→column, steps north→row; state location of tortoise (4,1); identify what is at (1,4).

items.prompt: On a zoo grid, the Tiger is at position (9, 5). How many steps East and how many steps North from the entrance do you move to reach the Tiger?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9 steps East, 5 steps North. The first number (9) is the column — East steps; the second number (5) is the row — North steps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the ordered pair as (East steps, North steps): first number = steps East, second number = steps North.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child reversed the pair, reading the second number as East and the first as North.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child used the first number (9) for both directions, ignoring the second number.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child used the second number (5) for both directions, ignoring the first number.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the pair as (East: 9, North: 5) and ask the child to copy just the East number; stretch: ask them to write the ordered pair for a point 3 steps East and 11 steps North.

exercise.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q1, p.178
exercise.description: Locate the animal at positions (11,11), (2,6), (6,4), (3,10), (11,3), (10,9) on the zoo grid map.

items.prompt: A Zebra is 6 steps East and 8 steps North of the entrance on a zoo grid. Write the ordered pair that gives the Zebra's position.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write (East steps, North steps): East = 6 goes first, North = 8 goes second.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give a partially completed pair (6, ___) and ask the child to fill in the North number; stretch: ask what animal would be at (8, 6) and whether that is the same position as (6, 8).

exercise.book_ref: Locating the Animals in the Zoological Park (Zoo) Q2, p.178
exercise.description: Write the ordered-pair position of Lion, Elephant, Tortoise, Deer, Panda, and Crocodile on the zoo map.
